spec.context_summary: This stress test examines how Mississauga's grid, operated by Alectra Utilities, would hold up under a repeat of the January 2014 polar vortex. A five-day Arctic outbreak that drove temperatures down to -25.5Â°C. Projected against a 2030 electrification landscape where 30% of homes use heat pumps and 30% of vehicles are electric. At those adoption levels, cold-weather demand spikes become significantly more severe, because heat pumps draw heavily on electricity precisely when temperatures plunge, compounding the load surge that extreme winter events already impose. The goal is to identify whether the distribution network has sufficient capacity to serve that future mix of customers without voltage collapse, transformer overload, or cascading outages. Understanding this risk now gives planners and regulators the lead time needed to invest in the right infrastructure upgrades before electrification reaches that scale.

cold_event.name: January 2014 Polar Vortex
cold_event.description: A high-amplitude Arctic outbreak that displaced the polar vortex southward, producing the coldest sustained period in Eastern Canada in 20+ years. IESO reported a winter peak of 23,127 MW on Jan 7. Heat pump-equipped homes saw widespread auxiliary resistance heat engagement. Used as the canonical 'severe event' baseline.

At 21 years old (age_years) with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False), this feeder already carries 1,224 customers (customers) and a 5% heat-pump share (heating_mix) that would scale dramatically under a 30% HP scenario, while 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct) adds coincident evening load with no capacity buffer from a prior upgrade.

This 24-year-old (age_years), never-upgraded (had_upgrade: False) feeder serves 1,360 customers (customers) with a 6% existing heat-pump share (heating_mix) that would multiply under a 30% HP scenario, and its 38.1% baseline utilization (utilization_pct) leaves limited headroom before the added 30% EV load pushes it toward overload.

At 27 years old (age_years) with no upgrade history (had_upgrade: False) and the highest customer count so far at 1,496 (customers), the 15% baseboard share (heating_mix) converting to heat pumps under the 30% HP scenario combined with 4.2% EV load (ev_pct) threatens an asset already at 42.3% utilization (utilization_pct).

This is the highest-risk feeder in the group: 30 years old (age_years), never upgraded (had_upgrade: False), serving 1,632 customers (customers) at 45.6% baseline utilization (utilization_pct), with a 5% existing heat-pump share (heating_mix) that would surge under a 30% HP scenario alongside 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct), leaving the least remaining capacity margin.

At 33 years old (age_years) with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False), this feeder's aging infrastructure is exposed to a 6% existing heat-pump share (heating_mix) scaling to 30% HP, and while its 30.5% utilization (utilization_pct) appears modest, the combination with 4.2% EV load (ev_pct) on degraded aging equipment elevates failure risk.

Now 36 years old (age_years) and never upgraded (had_upgrade: False), this feeder's 15% baseboard share (heating_mix) represents a large block of load that could electrify under the 30% HP scenario, and with 1,224 customers (customers) and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct) its aging conductors and equipment face compounding stress.

Despite a prior upgrade (had_upgrade: True), this feeder is 39 years old (age_years). The oldest in the dataset. And its 5% existing heat-pump share (heating_mix) across 1,360 customers (customers) would grow substantially under a 30% HP scenario, with 4.2% EV load (ev_pct) adding coincident demand on infrastructure that is typically near end-of-life at this age.

Although upgraded (had_upgrade: True) and only 18 years old (age_years), this feeder's 15% baseboard electric heating share (heating_mix) across 1,088 customers (customers) would convert to higher-draw heat pumps under the 30% HP scenario, and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct) adds simultaneous evening load that could erode its current 30.7% utilization (utilization_pct) headroom.

At 21 years old (age_years) with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False), a 5% existing heat-pump share (heating_mix) that would scale to 30% under the scenario, and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct) across 1,224 customers (customers), this feeder faces compounding electric load growth on aging, unimproved infrastructure currently sitting at 34.2% utilization (utilization_pct).

mitigations.title: Residential demand response enrollment on feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03
mitigations.rationale: Enrolling approximately 600 customers across the three flagged feeders (drawn from the 1,360 customers on MIS-01-F03, 1,224 on MIS-01-F02, and the customer base of MIS-01-F01 per top_3_at_risk_feeders customers fields) in a direct load control program targeting electric water heaters and smart thermostats would provide dispatchable load relief during peak hours. At a conservative enrollment cost of $300 per customer (industry rule of thumb for Canadian DR programs), 600 enrollments totals $180,000 CAD. This is the fastest deployable mitigation and does not require capital construction.

mitigations.title: Reconductor feeder MIS-01-F03
mitigations.rationale: Feeder MIS-01-F03 is the highest-utilization of the three flagged assets at 38.1% (utilization_pct), is 24 years old (age_years), has never been upgraded (had_upgrade: False), and serves 1,360 customers (customers). Reconductoring with a higher-ampacity conductor would increase thermal capacity and reduce the probability of overload under a 30% HP / 30% EV scenario. A single-feeder reconductor in the Ontario context typically costs $0.5â€“2M; $1.2M CAD is a conservative mid-range estimate for a feeder of this age and customer density. This is the highest-priority capital action given the combination of age, utilization, and load growth exposure.

mitigations.title: Reconductor feeder MIS-01-F02
mitigations.rationale: Feeder MIS-01-F02 is 21 years old (age_years), has had no prior upgrade (had_upgrade: False), operates at 34.2% utilization (utilization_pct), and serves 1,224 customers (customers). Its 5% existing heat pump share (heating_mix) would scale significantly under a 30% HP scenario. Reconductoring is warranted given the absence of any upgrade history and the projected load growth. Estimated at $1.0M CAD, consistent with the $0.5â€“2M Canadian feeder reconductor range for a feeder of moderate length and customer count.

mitigations.title: Time-of-use EV charging load shift program
mitigations.rationale: The Custom scenario assumes 30% EV penetration (scenario ev_pct), which contributes coincident evening load on top of heating demand. A managed charging program that shifts EV charging from the 5â€“9 PM peak window to overnight hours (11 PMâ€“6 AM) would reduce coincident peak exposure across all 176 feeders (network feeders). Program administration and customer incentive costs are estimated at $95,000 CAD for an initial cohort, consistent with industry rule-of-thumb program costs for managed EV charging pilots in comparable Canadian jurisdictions. This measure complements the demand response program and requires no physical infrastructure.

mitigations.title: Substation transformer capacity assessment and targeted upgrade at highest-load substations
mitigations.rationale: The model covers 22 substations (network substations) but does not include substation transformer thermal limits, which in comparable Ontario distribution systems are often the binding constraint before feeder-level limits are reached. A formal capacity assessment of the substations serving feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03 should be completed first; if transformer headroom is insufficient to support the 30% HP / 30% EV scenario, a transformer upgrade at one or two substations would provide the largest single increment of system-level risk reduction. Transformer upgrades in Canada typically cost $1â€“5M; $3.5M CAD reflects a conservative estimate for upgrading one substation transformer with associated protection and control work. This is the longest lead-time item and should be initiated in parallel with the reconductoring program.

result.executive_summary:
# Executive Summary: Mississauga Grid Resilience Under 30% Heat Pump / 30% EV Electrification Scenario

**Headline Finding**

The Alectra Utilities distribution network in Mississauga passes the User-specified (30% HP, 30% EV) electrification scenario, meaning modeled system-level capacity is sufficient under the conditions tested. But this result depends heavily on synthesized network data and does not eliminate feeder-level risk.

**Scenario Evidence**

Under the Custom scenario (30% heat pump, 30% EV penetration), the modeled system peak reaches 3,387.1 MW (scenario peak_mw) at hour 43 of the stress event, coinciding with a temperature of -28.0Â°C (scenario peak_temp_c). Against a baseline winter peak of 3,855.4 MW (network baseline_winter_peak_mw), the model shows 3,387.1 MW of headroom (scenario headroom_mw), representing 3387.5% of available capacity (scenario headroom_pct). The system-level verdict is PASS, and zero feeders are flagged as at-risk in aggregate (scenario at_risk_feeders: 0). However, the stress event modeled. The January 2014 Polar Vortex, with a minimum temperature of -25.5Â°C sustained over 120 hours (cold_event min_temp_c and duration_hours). Is a severe but historically observed benchmark, not a worst-case bound.

**At-Risk Assets**

Despite the system-level PASS, three feeders warrant targeted attention. Feeder MIS-01-F03 (Mississauga TS 01 F03) carries 1,360 customers (top_3_at_risk_feeders customers) at 38.1% baseline utilization (utilization_pct), is 24 years old (age_years), has never been upgraded (had_upgrade: False), and already has a 6% heat pump share (heating_mix) that would scale materially under a 30% HP scenario. Feeder MIS-01-F02 serves 1,224 customers (customers) at 34.2% utilization (utilization_pct) with no prior upgrade (had_upgrade: False) and is 21 years old (age_years). Feeder MIS-01-F01, while recently upgraded (had_upgrade: True), sits at 30.7% utilization (utilization_pct) with a 15% baseboard electric heating share (heating_mix) that creates stacking risk under simultaneous HP and EV load growth. Across all 3 feeders (network feeders) serving 230,384 customers (network customers), these three represent the leading edge of asset-age and load-growth exposure.

**Caveats and Limitations**

The network data is flagged as synthesized (network is_synthesized: True), meaning per-feeder utilization, customer counts, and age values are modeled estimates rather than confirmed asset records. System-level headroom of 1,557.8 MW (scenario headroom_mw) may overstate true available capacity if transformer or substation constraints. Not captured in this feeder-level model. Bind earlier. The analysis covers 22 substations (network substations) but does not include transmission-side constraints, protection coordination limits, or voltage profile degradation under cold-load pickup conditions, which industry experience suggests can be binding in polar vortex events even when thermal headroom appears adequate.

**Recommended Next Action**

Alectra should immediately commission field verification of asset records for feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS3387-F03, replacing synthesized values with actual nameplate ratings, protection settings, and maintenance histories. In parallel, the planning team should initiate a demand response enrollment program targeting residential customers on these three feeders ahead of the next heating season, and develop a capital prioritization plan for reconductoring MIS-01-F02 and MIS-01-F03 given their age and absence of prior upgrades. A full power-flow study incorporating voltage and protection constraints across all 22 substations (network substations) should be completed before any electrification incentive program exceeds 15% heat pump penetration in affected load zones.
result.methodology_notes: Peak load was estimated using a deterministic load model that applies electrification scenario penetration rates (heat pump percentage and EV percentage) to the baseline winter peak of 3,855.4 MW (network baseline_winter_peak_mw), with heat pump contributions adjusted via COP curves calibrated to the stress-event temperature profile of the January 2014 Polar Vortex (minimum -25.5Â°C over 120 hours). Per-feeder utilization, customer counts, and asset age values are synthesized model outputs (network is_synthesized: True) and have not been validated against Alectra Utilities' physical asset registry. Feeder-level risk rationales are therefore indicative and should be treated as prioritization signals for field verification rather than confirmed engineering assessments.
safety_flags: A 120-hour sustained cold event at -25.5Â°C (cold_event duration_hours and min_temp_c) creates life-safety risk for customers dependent on electrically powered medical devices such as home oxygen concentrators and dialysis equipment; Alectra should cross-reference its medical baseline registry against customers served by feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03 before the next heating season.

Mississauga's 230,384 customers (network customers) include a statistically significant elderly and low-income population who may lack backup heating; a prolonged outage during a polar vortex event of this magnitude (120 hours, -25.5Â°C per cold_event fields) could produce hypothermia casualties, and Alectra should coordinate warming centre activation protocols with the City of Mississauga emergency management office.

Cold-load pickup following any restoration event during a polar vortex can produce inrush currents that exceed feeder ratings even when pre-event utilization appears low; feeders MIS-01-F02 and MIS-01-F03, which have no upgrade history (had_upgrade: False), are at elevated risk of protection trips during re-energization and should be included in Alectra's staged restoration sequencing plan.
limitations: All per-feeder values including utilization percentages, customer counts, and asset ages are synthesized (network is_synthesized: True) and may not reflect actual field conditions; conclusions drawn from these values should be treated as hypotheses requiring validation against Alectra's asset management system before capital decisions are made.

The model does not account for transmission-side constraints, substation transformer thermal limits, voltage regulation limits, or protection coordination boundaries across the 22 substations (network substations); system-level headroom of 1,557.8 MW (scenario headroom_mw) could be materially reduced once these constraints are incorporated into a full power-flow study.

The scenario tests a single deterministic electrification penetration point (30% HP, 30% EV) against one historical stress event; it does not represent a probabilistic distribution of outcomes, and actual peak demand under a future polar vortex could differ based on building envelope improvements, EV charging behavior, or temperatures more extreme than the -25.5Â°C minimum observed in January 2014 (cold_event min_temp_c).
